_meta.description: Canonical error dictionary for the BET VM and Ternlang compiler. Every code maps to a fun message, a technical explanation, the most common causes, a concrete fix, and a runnable .tern example.

namespaces.PARSE: Lexer / parser phase — caught before any bytecode is emitted
namespaces.TYPE: Semantic analysis phase — type-checker caught a mismatch
namespaces.SCOPE: Name resolution — variable or binding not found
namespaces.BET: BET VM runtime errors — the bytecode is running and something went wrong

reserved_namespaces.IMPORT: Module import errors — reserved for when the module system is formalized (IMPORT-001: module not found, IMPORT-002: circular import)
reserved_namespaces.ANNOT: Annotation misuse — reserved for @sparseskip on non-matmul functions and future annotation validators (ANNOT-001)
reserved_namespaces.WARN: Non-fatal warnings — reserved for deprecation notices, performance hints, and style guidance (WARN-001 and above)
reserved_namespaces.CODE: Codegen internal errors — reserved for bugs in the bytecode emitter that don't map to a source error (CODE-001 and above)
reserved_namespaces.HDL: Hardware description language errors — reserved for ternlang-hdl crate (HDL-001 and above)
reserved_namespaces.MCP: Model Context Protocol errors — reserved for ternlang-mcp crate (MCP-001 and above)
reserved_namespaces.NET: Network / distributed agent errors — reserved for remote TSEND/TAWAIT over ternlang-net (NET-001 and above)

_meta.cli_lookup: ternlang errors <CODE>  — future CLI subcommand for interactive lookup (planned, not yet implemented)

PARSE-001.title: Unexpected Token
PARSE-001.fun_message: The lexer hit something it didn't expect and entered a hold state. It's not angry — just confused.
PARSE-001.technical: The tokenizer encountered a character or keyword sequence that does not fit any valid grammar production at this position in the source file.
common_causes: Typo in a keyword (e.g. 'fn' written as 'func' or 'def')
Using a symbol that doesn't exist in .tern syntax (e.g. '==', '&&', '||')
Forgetting a semicolon so the next line's token is read as a continuation
Using a binary language construct (true/false, null, None)
PARSE-001.fix: Read the error location, look at the offending token, and check the syntax reference. Most of the time it is a keyword typo or a missing semicolon on the line above.
PARSE-001.binary_habit_warning: Coming from Python/JS/Rust? Remember: no 'true'/'false' (use 1/-1), no '&&'/'||' (use 'consensus'), no 'null'/'None' (use 'hold()').

PARSE-002.title: Expected Token Not Found
PARSE-002.fun_message: The grammar was expecting something specific — like a closing brace or a type annotation — and got nothing. The compiler is not a mind reader.
PARSE-002.technical: The parser was in a state where exactly one token was valid next (e.g. ':' after a variable name, '{' after a match arm) and found something else instead.
common_causes: Missing type annotation on a 'let' declaration (e.g. 'let x = 1;' instead of 'let x: trit = 1;')
Missing closing brace '}' for a function or match block
Missing '->' return type in a function signature
Missing ':' separator in a match arm
PARSE-002.fix: The error message names exactly what was expected. Find the position, add the missing token.

PARSE-003.title: Invalid Trit Literal
PARSE-003.fun_message: Trits are -1, 0, or +1. There is no trit 2. There is no trit 'true'. The universe has three states. You tried to invent a fourth.
PARSE-003.technical: A trit literal was parsed but the value was not -1, 0, or +1. This includes using boolean literals ('true'/'false'), integers outside the ternary range, or string representations.
common_causes: Writing 'true' or 'false' where a trit is expected (binary habit)
Writing '2' or '-2' as a trit value
Confusing trit literals with int literals in a typed context
PARSE-003.fix: Use exactly -1, 0, or 1 as trit literals. Use the semantic helpers truth(), hold(), conflict() for readability.
PARSE-003.bad_pattern: let signal: trit = true;   // 'true' is not a trit
PARSE-003.good_pattern:
let signal: trit = 1;      // affirm
let signal: trit = truth(); // same thing, more readable

PARSE-004.title: Non-Exhaustive Match
PARSE-004.fun_message: Ternary has three states. You covered two. The compiler isn't being pedantic — the third state WILL occur at runtime. What happens then?
PARSE-004.technical: A match expression on a trit value did not include handlers for all three possible values (-1, 0, +1). Unlike binary switch-cases, ternary match is always exhaustive — there is no implicit default.
common_causes: Writing only -1 and 1 arms and forgetting the 0 (hold) case
Treating trit like a boolean and handling only two states
Copy-pasting a binary if/else pattern as a 2-arm match
PARSE-004.fix: Add the missing arm. Every match must handle -1, 0, and 1. The 0 state is the whole point of ternary — it is not an edge case.
PARSE-004.philosophy: The hold state (0) is not an error condition. It means 'insufficient evidence to commit.' Ignoring it is the mistake ternary logic was designed to prevent.

TYPE-001.title: Type Mismatch (Semantic)
TYPE-001.fun_message: You declared one type and handed in another. The type-checker caught it before the VM ever saw it. Consider this a gift.
TYPE-001.technical: The semantic analysis phase determined that the inferred or declared type of an expression does not match the expected type at this usage site. Caught at compile time, not runtime.
common_causes: Assigning an int literal to a trit variable (e.g. 'let x: trit = 42;')
Returning a trit from a function declared '-> int'
Passing a float to a function that expects a trit
TYPE-001.fix: Match the type of the value to the declared type. Use explicit conversion if needed.
TYPE-001.bad_pattern: let x: trit = 42;   // 42 is an int, not a trit
TYPE-001.good_pattern:
let x: trit = 1;    // valid trit
let n: int  = 42;   // valid int

SCOPE-001.title: Undefined Variable
SCOPE-001.fun_message: Hold state — '{name}' doesn't exist in this scope. You can't use a truth you never declared.
SCOPE-001.technical: The name resolver looked up the identifier in all enclosing scopes and found no declaration. The variable was either never declared, declared in a different scope that has ended, or has a typo.
common_causes: Typo in the variable name
Using a variable before its 'let' declaration
Referencing a variable declared inside a match arm from outside it
Forgetting to pass a value as a function argument
SCOPE-001.fix: Declare the variable with 'let' before using it, or check for a typo in the name.
SCOPE-001.bad_pattern: let result: trit = process(signal);  // 'signal' never declared
SCOPE-001.good_pattern:
let signal: trit = 1;
let result: trit = process(signal);

STRUCT-001.title: Undefined Struct
STRUCT-001.fun_message: The type system looked for this struct everywhere and found nothing. A ghost type — it doesn't exist.
STRUCT-001.technical: An identifier was used as a struct type in a declaration or constructor expression, but no struct with that name was defined in scope.
common_causes: Typo in the struct name
Using a struct from a module that wasn't imported
Defining the struct after its first use (forward reference)
STRUCT-001.fix: Define the struct before using it, or import the module that contains it.
STRUCT-001.bad_pattern:
// using TritSignal without defining it
let s: TritSignal = TritSignal { value: 1 };
STRUCT-001.good_pattern:
struct TritSignal { value: trit }
let s: TritSignal = TritSignal { value: 1 };

STRUCT-002.title: Undefined Struct Field
STRUCT-002.fun_message: '{struct}' exists, but it has no field called '{field}'. Check your struct definition — maybe the field was renamed or never added.
STRUCT-002.technical: A field access expression (struct.field) referenced a field name that is not present in the struct's definition.
common_causes: Typo in the field name
The field was removed from the struct definition but access code was not updated
Confusing two similar struct types
STRUCT-002.fix: Check the struct definition and use the correct field name.

FN-001.title: Undefined Function
FN-001.fun_message: '{name}' was called but never defined. You can't invoke a function that doesn't exist — even in ternary, three states don't include 'imaginary'.
FN-001.technical: A call expression referenced a function name that has no corresponding 'fn' declaration in scope and is not a built-in.
common_causes: Typo in the function name
Calling a function before its declaration (forward call without declaration)
Forgetting to import a module that defines the function
Renaming a function but not updating all call sites
FN-001.fix: Declare the function before calling it, or fix the typo in the call.
FN-001.bad_pattern: let x: trit = evaluate(1);  // 'evaluate' never defined

FN-002.title: Return Type Mismatch
FN-002.fun_message: You promised to return a {expected} but handed back a {found}. Ternary contracts are strict. The function signature is a promise.
FN-002.technical: A function declared a return type with '-> TYPE' but one of its return paths returns a value of a different type.
common_causes: A function declared '-> trit' returns an int literal
A match arm returns a different type than the others
Forgetting to convert a computed value before returning
FN-002.fix: Ensure every return path in the function returns the declared type.

FN-003.title: Argument Count Mismatch
FN-003.fun_message: '{name}' expects {expected} argument(s). You passed {found}. Arity is not optional — not even in hold state.
FN-003.technical: A function call passed a different number of arguments than the function's declaration specifies. Unlike some dynamic languages, Ternlang has no optional arguments or variadics at the call site.
common_causes: Forgetting an argument in a call
Passing an extra argument not in the signature
Calling a function after its signature was changed
FN-003.fix: Count the parameters in the 'fn' declaration and match them exactly at the call site.

FN-004.title: Argument Type Mismatch
FN-004.fun_message: Argument {index} of '{name}' should be a {expected}, but you passed a {found}. Types travel with their values — they don't change at the border.
FN-004.technical: One or more arguments in a function call have a type that does not match the corresponding parameter type in the function's declaration.
common_causes: Passing an int literal where a trit is expected
Passing a float result to a function expecting trit
Mixing up argument order between two similar-typed parameters
FN-004.fix: Check the function signature, then ensure each argument's type matches its parameter type.
FN-004.bad_pattern:
fn signal(v: trit) -> trit { return v; }
let r: trit = signal(99);  // 99 is int, fn expects trit
FN-004.good_pattern:
fn signal(v: trit) -> trit { return v; }
let r: trit = signal(1);   // 1 is a valid trit

PROP-001.title: Propagation on Non-Trit
PROP-001.fun_message: The '?' operator only works on trit-returning expressions. You used it on a {found}. The third state requires a trit — you can't propagate uncertainty from a type that has none.
PROP-001.technical: The '?' postfix operator, which propagates a -1 (conflict) result up the call stack early, was applied to an expression whose type is not 'trit'. Only trit-typed expressions carry the three-valued signal needed for propagation.
common_causes: Applying '?' to an int-returning function call
Applying '?' to a float expression
Confusing '?' with error propagation in other languages (Rust's '?' works on Result, Ternlang's works on trit)
PROP-001.fix: Only apply '?' to function calls or expressions that return trit.
PROP-001.bad_pattern:
fn get_count() -> int { return 5; }
let x: int = get_count()?;  // '?' on int — not valid
PROP-001.good_pattern:
fn check() -> trit { return truth(); }
let x: trit = check()?;     // '?' on trit — valid

BET-001.title: Stack Underflow
BET-001.fun_message: You tried to pop a truth that wasn't there. The VM's stack is empty — like asking someone to give back a hug they never received.
BET-001.technical: A TPOP, TRET, or arithmetic instruction was executed when the VM's operand stack contained zero values. The stack depth went below zero.
common_causes: A function exits without pushing a return value (missing 'return' on a code path)
A match arm falls through without returning
A codegen bug emitting more POPs than PUSHes in a loop or branch
BET-001.fix: Ensure every code path through every function ends with an explicit 'return'. In match expressions, every arm must return.
BET-001.note: If you are writing .tern code normally and hit this, it almost always means a missing return in a match arm. If you're editing core codegen and hit this, count your TPUSH/TPOP pairs.

BET-002.title: BET Encoding Fault
BET-002.fun_message: The 0b00 bit pattern is forbidden in balanced ternary encoding. Only 01 (-1), 10 (0), and 11 (+1) exist. You found the state that shouldn't be — the void.
BET-002.technical: The BET codec encountered the 0b00 two-bit pattern while unpacking a packed trit byte. This pattern is undefined in the BET encoding scheme, where every trit uses 2 bits with values 01, 10, or 11.
common_causes: Memory corruption in the bytecode buffer
Manually crafted .ternbc bytecode with an invalid trit encoding
A bug in a custom BET serializer/deserializer
BET-002.fix: Recompile from source. If you're working at the bytecode level, use only 01/10/11 patterns for trit encoding. Never write 00.

BET-003.title: Clean Halt
BET-003.fun_message: Execution reached the end. This is not an error — this is peace. The VM executed your program completely and stopped cleanly.
BET-003.technical: The VM encountered the THALT opcode or reached the end of the bytecode buffer with no pending instructions. This is the normal, successful termination condition.
common_causes: Program ran to completion successfully
BET-003.fix: No fix needed. This is success.
BET-003.note: If BET-003 appears in a context where you expected the program to keep running, check whether your main logic is accidentally being skipped by an early return.

BET-004.title: Unknown Opcode
BET-004.fun_message: The machine is reading your bytecode and hit an instruction it has never seen. This opcode belongs to a future version of the VM — or to a file that got corrupted. Recompile.
BET-004.technical: The VM's instruction dispatch loop encountered a byte value that does not correspond to any opcode in the BET ISA (Instruction Set Architecture). The bytecode is either corrupted, from a different VM version, or manually crafted incorrectly.
common_causes: Stale .ternbc file compiled with an older or newer compiler version
Manually editing a .ternbc file and introducing an invalid byte
Encoding mismatch between codegen and VM opcode table
BET-004.fix: Delete any cached .ternbc files and recompile from source with 'ternlang-cli'. Always recompile after upgrading the compiler.

BET-005.title: Register Out of Range
BET-005.fun_message: The BET VM has exactly 27 registers — 3³, the only sacred ternary number. You tried to access register {reg}, which doesn't exist. There is no 28th register.
BET-005.technical: An instruction referenced a register index outside the range 0–26. The BET VM's register file is fixed at 27 entries (3³), addressable as indices 0–26.
common_causes: A codegen bug emitting a register index above 26
Manually crafted bytecode with an out-of-range register operand
A register allocation bug in an experimental compiler extension
BET-005.fix: If you're writing .tern source code, this error is not your fault — it's a compiler bug. Report it. If you're building a codegen extension, clamp all register allocations to 0–26.

BET-006.title: PC Out of Bounds
BET-006.fun_message: The program counter jumped to address {pc} — which is outside the bytecode buffer. You jumped into the void. The universe ends at the last instruction.
BET-006.technical: A jump instruction (TJMP, TJMP_NEG, TJMP_POS, TCALL, etc.) set the program counter to an address that exceeds the length of the loaded bytecode. Execution cannot continue.
common_causes: A stale .ternbc file with jump targets calculated for a different (longer or shorter) bytecode layout
A codegen bug emitting an incorrect jump offset
Manually patching bytecode without recalculating jump offsets
BET-006.fix: Recompile from source. Jump targets are absolute offsets calculated at compile time — any change to the bytecode invalidates them unless recompiled.

BET-007.title: Runtime Type Mismatch
BET-007.fun_message: Square peg, round hole. The VM expected a {expected} on the stack but found a {found}. The types got mixed somewhere between the call site and the instruction.
BET-007.technical: A VM instruction that expects a specific Value variant (e.g., Trit, Int, TensorRef) was executed but found a different variant on the stack. This is the runtime version of TYPE-001 — it slipped past the static checker.
common_causes: A function returning a mixed type depending on the code path (one arm returns trit, another returns int)
Calling a built-in with the wrong argument type
A codegen gap where the type annotation was missing and the wrong opcode was emitted
BET-007.fix: Trace back to where the mismatched value was produced. Add explicit type annotations to declarations to help the compiler catch this at TYPE-001 instead of here.
BET-007.note: If you see BET-007 where you did not see TYPE-001, it means the type checker missed a path. That is a compiler bug — please report it with the .tern source that triggers it.

BET-008.title: Tensor Index Out of Bounds
BET-008.fun_message: Tensor[N]: index K is out of bounds — tensor only has M element(s). Trittensors don't grow on access.
BET-008.technical: A TIDX (read) or TSET (write) instruction computed an element position that is >= the tensor's allocated size. The VM performs a bounds check and refuses to fabricate trit values for memory it doesn't own.
common_causes: Zero-based indexing confusion: trittensor<N> has valid indices 0 through N-1, not 0 through N
Off-by-one in a loop counter that reaches the tensor's size
Accessing a 2D tensor with indices that exceed the row×column layout
BET-008.fix: Check that your index is strictly less than the tensor's declared size. Use guard conditionals before every tensor access in dynamic code.
BET-008.index_rule: trittensor<N>: valid indices are 0 to N-1. Index N is always out of bounds.

BET-009.title: Tensor Not Allocated
BET-009.fun_message: TensorRef(N) doesn't exist — you never allocated it. TALLOC first, then TIDX.
BET-009.technical: A TIDX, TSET, or TSHAPE instruction received a TensorRef ID that exceeds the number of tensors in the VM's tensor table. The allocation step (TALLOC) was never executed for this slot.
common_causes: In normal .tern code: a compiler bug where TALLOC was not emitted for a trittensor declaration — please report
In manual bytecode: TIDX executed before the corresponding TALLOC on a code path that was conditional
A TensorRef value was copied but points to a tensor that was allocated in a different VM instance
BET-009.fix: In .tern code: recompile from source. If BET-009 persists from valid .tern, it is a compiler bug — report with the triggering source. In manual bytecode: ensure TALLOC always executes before TIDX on every code path.

BET-010.title: Agent Type Not Registered
BET-010.fun_message: Agent type_id 0xNNNN was never registered. You can't spawn what was never declared.
BET-010.technical: The TSPAWN instruction received a type_id (u16) that has no entry in the VM's agent type table (agent_types HashMap). TSPAWN cannot create an agent instance without knowing which bytecode address to jump to for its handler.
common_causes: An 'agent' declaration is missing from the program — the type was used but never defined
The agent was defined in a module that was not imported or loaded
The CLI's register_agent_type() was not called for this type_id (codegen gap)
BET-010.fix: Declare the agent with 'agent MyAgent { ... }' before spawning it. Import the module containing the declaration if it's defined externally.

BET-011.title: Agent ID Invalid
BET-011.fun_message: Agent #N doesn't exist — no agent was spawned at this ID. TSEND and TAWAIT require a live agent.
BET-011.technical: A TSEND or TAWAIT instruction received an AgentRef with an ID >= the number of agents in the VM's agent table. The agent at that ID was never spawned, or the AgentRef was constructed with an incorrect ID.
common_causes: In normal .tern code: a compiler bug where an incorrect AgentRef ID was emitted — please report
In manual bytecode: TSEND executed with an AgentRef ID that was never returned by TSPAWN
A TSPAWN failed (BET-010) and the returned invalid AgentRef was used anyway
BET-011.fix: Always use the AgentRef value returned by the 'spawn' expression. Do not construct AgentRef values manually. Ensure TSPAWN succeeds (no BET-010) before calling TSEND or TAWAIT.
BET-011.distinction_from_bet_010: BET-010 = the agent TYPE was never registered (spawn fails). BET-011 = the agent INSTANCE doesn't exist (send/await fails on a bad ID).

BET-012.title: Division by Zero
BET-012.fun_message: Ternary division by zero. The universe cannot divide by zero — not even in a hold state. Every state requires a non-zero denominator.
BET-012.technical: A TDIV or TMOD instruction was executed when the second operand (denominator) was exactly zero (Int(0) or Float(0.0)).
common_causes: Using an uninitialized variable that defaults to zero in a division
Dividing by a computed result that happened to be zero
Failure to bound-check a denominator before division
BET-012.fix: Always check that your denominator is not zero before performing a division or modulo operation.

BET-013.title: Call Stack Overflow
BET-013.fun_message: VM Error: [BET-013] Call stack overflow — max depth (4096) exceeded. Infinite recursion or unbounded cross-module mutual calls detected.
BET-013.technical: The VM's call stack reached its maximum depth of 4096. This almost always means an infinite recursion (a function calling itself) or a circular dependency between multiple functions.
common_causes: Infinite Recursion: A function calls itself with no base case or a base case that is never reached.
Mutual Recursion: Function A calls B, and B calls A.
Unresolved Imports: [FIXED 2026-04-13] A named import from a module where the imported function calls another local function that was NOT imported.
Broken Built-ins: [FIXED 2026-04-13] Calling 'shape(t)' or 'zeros(n)' which were stubs that triggered recursion or incorrect jumps. Use 'length(t)' instead.
BET-013.fix: Ensure recursive functions have a base case. Use 'import *' to pull in all local dependencies of functions. Check for circular module calls.
